issues.legal_issue: The Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 does not govern succession to the stridhan property of a Hindu female.
material_facts: The deceased died unmarried, and the Court considered the succession claim on the assumption that the property was her absolute, non-watan stridhan property.
The claimants invoked the 1929 Act to place a sister's sons ahead of a paternal uncle's son in the succession to her property.
issues.conclusion: The 1929 Act applies only to the separate property of a Hindu male dying intestate and cannot be invoked to determine heirs to a Hindu female's stridhan property.
issues.legal_principle: The preamble and section 1(2) of the Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929 limit its operation to succession to the separate property of a Hindu male dying intestate; it neither changes devolution of other property owned by a Hindu male nor regulates succession to a Hindu female's property. The Court approved Manda Mahalakshmamma v. Mantravadi, Shakuntalabai v. Court of Wards, Talukraj Kuer v. Bacha Kuer and Kuppuswami v. Manickasari, and did not approve Shamrao v. Raghunandan, Mst. Charjo v. Dinanath, Kehar Singh v. Attar Singh and Indra Pal v. Humangi Debi.

predicates.succession_claim_to_female_property: The proceeding concerns a claim to succeed to property left by a female.
predicates.female_property_is_stridhan: The female's property is treated as her stridhan property.
predicates.inheritance_amendment_is_invoked_to_rank: A claimant relies on an inheritance amendment to determine the order of heirs to the female's property.

issues.definition: When a succession claim concerns a female's stridhan and an inheritance amendment is invoked to rank her heirs, the amendment does not govern that succession.

issues.legal_issue: Under the Mitakshara and Mayukha rules applicable to a maiden's property, a paternal uncle's son takes precedence over a sister's son when succession reaches the father's sapindas.
material_facts: The deceased died a maiden, and the property was considered on the assumption that it was her absolute stridhan property.
The claimants were the deceased's father's sister's sons, while the rival claimant was her father's paternal uncle's son.
The competing claimants were treated as sapindas of the deceased's father, and the 1929 Act's altered order of heirs did not apply to succession to her property.
issues.conclusion: The paternal uncle's son had a preferential right to succeed over the sister's sons, so the claimants were not the nearest heirs even on the assumption that the property was the deceased's non-watan stridhan.
issues.legal_principle: Under the rule stated in Baudhayana and accepted by the commentators, a maiden's property passes first to her uterine brothers, then to her mother, then to her father; on their failure, it passes to the nearest relations, meaning the father's sapindas and, in their default, the mother's sapindas, in order of propinquity. Under the Mitakshara law, the paternal uncle's son follows the paternal uncle and ranks above a sister's son; the Mayukha law applicable in Bombay makes no difference to that ranking. The Court referred to Viramitrodaya and Mayne's Hindu Law, Article 621, and held that the 1929 Act did not alter this order for a female's stridhan.
